entries.short: Are you serious? / please be serious / come back to reality.
entries.origin: AAVE/texting → TikTok comment speech; get real is older English reply culture.

entries.short: Really good — especially music or a committed performance.
entries.origin: Music/hip-hop praise slang → general internet.

entries.explain: Fit check = show the clothes; drip = iced/stylish fashion.
entries.origin: Fashion social formats on TikTok/IG; drip from hip-hop slang.

entries.short: Throw with force — or general hype exclamation.
entries.origin: Vine/internet 2010s; still understood.
Vine viral comedy (Charles Black “What are those!”) mid-2010s.

entries.short: Dismissive reply to out-of-touch older takes.
entries.origin: 2019 viral intergenerational meme on TikTok/Reddit/Twitter.
Coined earlier, popularized ~2021 in TikTok/NYT discourse.

entries.short: Protected by the story — inexplicably can’t lose yet.
entries.explain: Anime/movie fan term for characters who survive for narrative reasons.
entries.origin: TV Tropes / fandom discourse → general meme use.

entries.short: Game metaphor: side quest = optional detour; main quest = the real priority.
entries.explain: Life planning jokes — studying is main quest, scrolling is side quest.
entries.origin: Gaming vocabulary → everyday Gen Z metaphor.

entries.short: Excited hype reaction from Twitch culture.
entries.origin: Twitch emotes (PogChamp) → wider gaming slang.

entries.short: Mad + balding — melting down in chat.
entries.origin: Twitch/Forsen community slang → wider gaming.

entries.short: Fake “medicine” for coping with loss — denial as a joke.
entries.explain: Esports/political meme: inhale copium when your team/fave is cooked.
entries.origin: Twitch/esports Wojak “copium” memes → general internet.

entries.short: Hardcore fan — to stan is to support obsessively (lovingly or ironically).
entries.explain: From Eminem’s song “Stan”; now general fandom verb.
entries.origin: Eminem “Stan” (2000) → Tumblr/Twitter fandom language.

entries.explain: Adds finality to a take. “Periodt” is the emphatic spelling.
entries.origin: AAVE / Black Twitter emphasis → general internet.

entries.short: Delivering a look or moment with intention — “serving looks.”
entries.explain: Closely related to “it’s giving” / ballroom performance language.
entries.origin: Ballroom culture → mainstream queer and TikTok slang.
Ballroom culture (documented in Paris Is Burning era) → mainstream pop culture.

entries.short: Tea = gossip; spilling tea = sharing it; sipping tea = watching drama.
entries.origin: Drag/LGBTQ+ and Black vernacular → RuPaul’s Drag Race popularization → mainstream.

entries.explain: Often with a hand gesture. Replaced older “damn” in some circles.
entries.origin: Rap/internet revival; TikTok dance/reaction wave ~2021.
New York AAVE/regional slang → wider internet.

entries.explain: Intensity dials for feelings and opinions.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream youth slang.

entries.short: Affects you more than usual — nostalgia or vibe upgrade.
entries.origin: AAVE-influenced casual speech → mainstream social captions.

entries.short: Unusually talented/tough — operating on another level.
entries.explain: Compliment or meme flex. Sometimes ironic.
entries.origin: Sports/internet praise phrase popularized in the late 2010s–2020s.

entries.short: You used to be better — quality or relevance dropped.
entries.explain: Music/career roast that applies to anyone.
entries.origin: Hip-hop discourse → general internet.

entries.short: Suddenly cut off communication without explanation.
entries.origin: 2010s dating slang → fully mainstream.

entries.short: A discreet hookup / person you see privately.
entries.explain: Usually low-key and not publicly claimed.
entries.origin: AAVE / youth slang → TikTok mainstream.

entries.short: Dating metaphor: warning sign (red), healthy sign (green), harmless odd quirk (beige).
entries.explain: Used way beyond dating too — any vibe check shorthand.
entries.origin: Relationship advice language → TikTok listicle culture; “beige flag” is a later playful addition.

entries.short: Sudden turn-off — a small thing that kills attraction.
entries.explain: Not always rational; that’s the point. Viral on dating TikTok.
entries.origin: British/pop dating slang popularized again via Love Island and TikTok explainers.

entries.short: More than friends, less than a defined relationship.
entries.explain: Ambiguous romantic/sexual gray zone. Extremely common Gen Z relationship word.
entries.origin: Dating-discourse slang popularized on Tumblr/Twitter/TikTok.

entries.explain: Modern dating pipeline step before official labels.
entries.origin: Gen Z dating vocabulary popularized on TikTok/Twitter.

entries.short: Soft launch = subtle partner cameo; hard launch = full public reveal.
entries.explain: Relationship posting strategy borrowed from product marketing.
entries.origin: Marketing terms applied to Instagram couple reveals; TikTok dating discourse.

entries.short: Self-labeling a life chapter — “in my healing era.”
entries.explain: Taylor Swift “eras” language + TikTok identity captions.
entries.origin: Pop fandom (esp. Swiftie “eras”) + TikTok “in my X era” format.

entries.short: Moment that feels permanently formative (Inside Out language).
entries.explain: Used earnestly or ironically for tiny events.
entries.origin: Pixar’s Inside Out popularized the phrase; TikTok made it caption slang.

entries.short: Thing you think about constantly — your recurring mental tab.
entries.explain: From the “how often do men think about the Roman Empire” viral prompt.
entries.origin: 2023 TikTok/Instagram viral question → general “my Roman Empire is X” format.

entries.short: Ironic trio flipping girlboss feminism into villain verbs; girlboss alone is ambition branding (often ironic now).
entries.explain: Joke slogan parodying toxic girlboss culture; “girlboss” started as empowerment branding.
entries.origin: Sophia Amoruso Girlboss branding → internet irony and the “gaslight gatekeep girlboss” meme.

terms: tell me you're ___ without telling me
entries.short: Meme prompt: reveal a trait via vibes, not a direct statement.
entries.explain: Fill-in format for identity jokes and soft callouts.
entries.origin: Viral Twitter/TikTok prompt format of the early 2020s.

entries.explain: Reaction to secondhand embarrassment or bad news.
entries.origin: Everyday slang amplified as a stock internet reaction.

entries.short: That’s a strange thing to brag about — but noted.
entries.explain: Mild clapback to an odd humblebrag or flex.
entries.origin: 2010s meme/reaction phrase on Twitter and Instagram.

entries.short: Extremely online — steeped in niche internet context.
entries.explain: Describes people (or yourself) who speak fluent meme. Not always an insult.
entries.origin: Internet self-awareness slang widely used on Twitter/TikTok.

entries.short: Exposed with clear evidence — no denials left.
entries.explain: Like “gotcha,” but cinematic. Screenshots and receipts energy.
entries.origin: Social-media callout slang; “4K” = ultra-clear proof. Viral on Twitter/TikTok.

entries.explain: Agreement that a take matches lived experience. More “true feelings” than media “real news.”
entries.origin: AAVE / casual speech → TikTok comment culture.

entries.short: Extra “for real” — serious emphasis / strong agreement.
entries.explain: Stacks “fr” twice. Softens or intensifies depending on tone.
entries.origin: AAVE → mainstream texting/TikTok; “fr” itself is older internet/texting shorthand.

entries.short: Secondhand embarrassment — something feels awkward, try-hard, or uncomfortably earnest.
entries.explain: Can be sincere or ironic. Overused as a dismissal; still the default word for painful awkwardness.
entries.origin: English “cringe” as internet judgment slang surged via early-2010s forums/YouTube; still core Gen Z vocabulary.

entries.short: Silhouette dance people do to “distract” — a recurring TikTok bit/sound.
entries.explain: Usually posted as a silly cutaway dance. More ritual than deep meaning.
entries.origin: Animated Distraction Dance meme audio/format popular on TikTok and YouTube Shorts.

entries.short: Kid’s joyful “It’s CORN!” song/meme — pure wholesome brainrot.
entries.explain: Referenced when something is unexpectedly hype about a mundane thing, or as a nostalgic TikTok sound callback.
entries.origin: Recreating Recording’s “It’s Corn” video that went mega-viral on TikTok/YouTube in 2022.

entries.short: VSCO-girl era fluster: catch yourself mid-spill or mid-giggle.
entries.explain: Often stacked with “sksksk.” Now partly nostalgic/ironic, still referenced.
entries.origin: VSCO girl meme wave (~2019); “and I oop” circulated via viral clips in that era.

entries.short: Please stop — polite-shaped, actually done with this.
entries.explain: Soft-sounding boundary with side-eye. Millennial/Gen Z texting staple.
entries.origin: Everyday English that became a stock reaction phrase on Tumblr/Twitter in the 2010s.

entries.short: Wojak template contrasting a mocked “average fan” with a chad “enjoyer.”
entries.explain: Format joke: paint one group as cringe average fans and another as chad enjoyers. Fill-in-the-blank meme grammar.
entries.origin: Wojak / “average X fan vs average Y enjoyer” template from meme boards → Reddit/Twitter.

entries.short: Wojak-style format: smiling in a crowd while privately knowing a niche fact/obsession.
entries.explain: Usually paired with a panel of a character thinking “they don’t know…” about a hyper-specific interest. About secret context, not literal stealth.
entries.origin: Feels Guy / Wojak “they don’t know” comic format popularized on meme communities and Twitter.

entries.short: Pretending everything’s okay while it’s clearly on fire.
entries.explain: Used when you’re calmly coping (or ironically not coping) through chaos.
entries.origin: KC Green’s webcomic “On Fire” (Gunshow, 2013) — the dog-in-a-burning-room panel became one of the internet’s core reaction memes.

entries.short: Playful admission of blank-brain mode — vibing, not thinking hard.
entries.explain: Self-deprecating or cute: you’re running on aesthetic, not analysis. Meme caption staple.
entries.origin: Tumblr/Twitter reaction caption culture; still used as a soft “brain offline” joke.

entries.short: I’m already in — no further explanation needed.
entries.explain: Agreement / green light. Close cousin of “bet.”
entries.origin: AAVE / hip-hop vernacular → broad Gen Z and TikTok use (say less); “say no more” is older English still used the same way.

entries.short: Someone/something is stuck in your head — occupying mental space for free.
entries.explain: “They’re living rent free in your head” = you’re still thinking about them more than they think about you.
entries.origin: Older idiom popularized as a stock internet dunk/self-own on Twitter and memes.

entries.short: Nailed the brief — did exactly what the moment called for (look, performance, vibe).
entries.explain: Compliment for hitting the mark. Often used for outfits, covers, or cameos.
entries.origin: Black Twitter / social praise phrase that went fully mainstream on Twitter and TikTok (~2020–21).

entries.short: Emphasis opener: “the way that I…” = I’m about to stress how hard something hits.
entries.explain: Stan/Twitter cadence that soft-launches a strong feeling (“the way I ran here”). Not a secret code.
entries.origin: Stan Twitter / Black Twitter phrasing patterns → general social media.

entries.short: Someone (often a fave) is serving excellence — serving “mother” energy.
entries.explain: Praise for competence, beauty, or dominance. “Mother” here is queer/stan honorific, not only literal mom.
entries.origin: Ballroom / drag / stan Twitter vocabulary → TikTok.

entries.short: Shocked, stunned, or impressed — speechless in a good (or dramatic) way.
entries.explain: Like “I’m shook,” but with more performance/shade energy. In ballroom/queer slang, gagging can mean stunned by a look or read.
entries.origin: Ballroom / Black LGBTQ+ slang → wider Twitter/TikTok use.

entries.short: Classic dunk stack: you took an L and got ratioed (replies crush likes).
entries.explain: Twitter/X clapback format. “Ratio” alone means reply-count humiliation; adding “L” piles on.
entries.origin: Twitter ratio culture; “L + ratio” became a stock reply format in the early 2020s.

entries.short: Dramatic (or joking) despair — the moment/team/life arc just died.
entries.explain: Hyperbolic “we’re cooked.” Frequently flipped seconds later into “we are so back.”
entries.origin: Older “it’s over” reaction memes; “it’s SO over” / over–back pairing surged on Twitter and meme communities in the early 2020s.

entries.short: Sudden optimism — the vibe, team, or fandom just got revived.
entries.explain: Said when something that looked doomed suddenly looks good again. Often paired with its twin “it’s so over.”
entries.origin: Internet doom/hope oscillation memes; paired with “it’s over / it’s so over” on Twitter/4chan-adjacent culture (~2021–23) then everywhere.

entries.short: Names the vibe something radiates — “it’s giving main character,” “it’s giving flop.”
entries.explain: A quick aesthetic/energy read. Often playful or shade-y. Related to “serving” / vibe language. Not literal “giving a gift.”
entries.origin: Black LGBTQ+ / ballroom and AAVE vernacular → Twitter/TikTok mainstream (esp. ~2020–21).
VSCO app + 2019 TikTok stereotype wave.

entries.short: Game + meme wave that made “sus” unavoidable; emergency meeting = call everyone now.
entries.explain: References the 2020 social-deduction boom and its UI jokes.
entries.origin: Among Us game virality (2020).

entries.short: Nerf = weaken; buff = strengthen; meta = current best strategies.
entries.explain: Game-balance words used for life (“they nerfed my sleep schedule”).
entries.origin: Gaming (esp. Nerf toy brand metaphor) → everyday internet.

entries.short: Finish as fast as possible — games, or metaphorically life tasks.
entries.origin: Speedrunning game community → general metaphor.

entries.short: Make ordinary life feel cinematic on purpose.
entries.explain: Self-care aesthetic trend — coffee, walks, journaling as movie scenes.
entries.origin: TikTok “romanticize your life” trend wave.

entries.short: Discourse tone tools: valid = fair; noted = acknowledged (sometimes cold); respectfully = softener before disagreement.
entries.explain: Common internet/conflict vocabulary with tone that depends on delivery.
entries.origin: Workplace and internet validation/conflict speak.

entries.short: Fixing to — about to / going to.
entries.explain: “I’m finna leave” = I’m about to leave.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider youth slang.

entries.short: Fax = facts — agreement. “No printer” setups the pun.
entries.origin: Internet pun culture on “fax/facts.”

entries.short: Opinion quality grades — L bad, W good, mid meh.
entries.origin: Sports/internet W/L culture applied to opinions on Twitter/TikTok.

entries.short: Not trying to be the center — supporting-role or extra vibe.
entries.explain: Can be humble or self-roast. Inverse of main character energy.
entries.origin: Main-character meme inverse; anime/gaming extras metaphor → TikTok.

entries.short: Overwhelmed reaction / shock at nerve / playful callout starter.
entries.explain: “I can’t even” = speechless overwhelm; “the audacity” = disbelief at nerve; “not the ___” points at a specific detail.
entries.origin: 2010s Tumblr/Twitter and Black Twitter reaction patterns still in heavy use.

entries.short: Defiant confidence after a challenge — “nope, I’d still win.” Often half-joke swagger (or ironic doom).
entries.explain: People drop “nah, I’d win” when they want Gojo-level cocky energy: someone asks if you’d lose, and you answer like defeat isn’t on the table. Online it’s also used ironically when you definitely will not win. Judgment-free: it’s a meme catchphrase, not a personality diagnosis.
entries.origin: Jujutsu Kaisen manga: Satoru Gojo’s line (notably Ch. 221 callback to Ch. 3). English “Nah, I’d win” wording spread via VIZ/fan translations; exploded as an exploitable panel + TikTok/anime-Twitter meme in late 2023.

entries.short: In meme slang: opposite of “alpha” — portrayed as passive or less dominant (often rude/joke).
entries.explain: Internet “beta” is usually an insult or ironic label in alpha/sigma meme talk — not the software “beta test” meaning, and not a clinical term. Judgment-free tip: people throw it around loosely; it’s more meme than science.
entries.origin: Same pop hierarchy memes as alpha; gaming/internet culture.

entries.short: In TikTok/internet slang: top-dog / “best” / dominant vibe — not the Greek letter.
entries.explain: Online, calling someone (or yourself) “alpha” usually means confident, high-status, in charge, or “that girl/guy is the best.” It’s meme language from manosphere/self-help crossover into general TikTok. Tone ranges from serious flex to ironic joke. Separately, alpha is also the first Greek letter and a software “early version” word — but if you saw it on TikTok, they almost certainly mean the slang status vibe.
entries.origin: Pop-psych “alpha/beta” animal hierarchy metaphors → internet debate culture → TikTok shorthand for elite/dominant energy.

entries.short: YouTube/TikTok horror-comedy series by DaFuq!?Boom! with heads in toilets; kids also chant “skibidi” as brainrot noise.
entries.explain: Skibidi Toilet is a surreal animated series by DaFuq!?Boom! (Alexey Gerasimov): singing human heads in toilets fight camera-headed people (Cameramen) and other hardware-headed factions. On playgrounds and the FYP, “skibidi” is often just a nonsense chant — participation, not a secret code. Asking what it means is normal; the joke is how little dictionary sense it has.
entries.origin: YouTube series by DaFuq!?Boom!, 2023–; exploded on TikTok and in Gen Alpha schoolyard/brainrot culture.

entries.short: Catch-all punchline for anything chaotic, cursed, or strangely specific — rarely about the actual state.
entries.explain: “Only in Ohio” = this could only happen in meme-Ohio. Often paired with other brainrot vocabulary.
entries.origin: TikTok / Gen Alpha absurdist meme where “Ohio” became shorthand for cursed Americana chaos (early–mid 2020s).

entries.short: A loud reaction to someone’s body, especially hips/backside — like an exaggerated “goddamn.”
entries.explain: Exclamation more than description. Common in stream culture and brainrot packs; can be objectifying — read the room.
entries.origin: Phonetic twist on “goddamn,” amplified by streamers/TikTok; entered Gen Alpha brainrot vocabulary.

entries.short: Playfully taking a bite of someone else’s food — a ‘tax’ named after streamer Fanum.
entries.explain: Friends joke-steal a fry/nugget and call it Fanum tax. Not a real fee.
entries.origin: Coined around AMP streamer Fanum’s habit of tasting friends’ food; exploded via TikTok/YouTube clips.

entries.short: Tongue-posture trend people claim will change a jawline.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing-adjacent tip: press tongue to palate. Evidence is contested; meme status is not.
entries.origin: Orthotropics (Mike Mew discourse) → TikTok looksmaxxing explainers and brainrot jokes.

entries.short: Internet slang for a lone-wolf “cool outsider” archetype (cousin of “alpha” memes).
entries.explain: On TikTok, “sigma” is a personality meme: independent, quiet-confident, not needing the crowd. Often half-joke. Related to alpha/beta meme vocabulary.
entries.origin: Online personality-type memes adjacent to alpha discourse; exploded on TikTok/Reels.

entries.short: Looking so much more attractive that you ‘mog’ someone else’s looks by comparison.
entries.explain: Looksmaxxing comparative slang. Can be joke or harsh ranking talk.
entries.origin: Looksmaxxing forum slang (AMOG / aesthetic mogging roots) → TikTok/brainrot speech.

entries.short: Trying to optimize appearance with routines, tips, and sometimes extreme advice.
entries.explain: Forum-to-TikTok pipeline. Ranges from skincare to controversial “maxxing” subcultures.
entries.origin: Looksmaxxing forums → TikTok explainers; paired with mewing/mogging vocabulary.

entries.short: Hovering at the edge of a payoff without finishing — a joke about delay and tension.
entries.explain: People say they’re edging when they stretch a wait (a reveal, a win, or an innuendo) without going over. In casual TikTok use it’s usually a bit, not a how-to. Keep it PG: the slang is about delay, not instructions.
entries.origin: Older slang recycled as a TikTok/stream joke.

entries.short: Quick social mood test — does this feel right?
entries.explain: Can be literal question or meme threat joke.
entries.origin: 2010s internet → still common on TikTok and in group chats.

entries.short: Content so absurd or repetitive it feels like it rewires your brain — often said with affection.
entries.explain: Label for hyper-online, low-context, loop-heavy meme speech (and for yourself when you’ve watched too much of it).
entries.origin: Older “brain rot” metaphor; Gen Alpha/TikTok FYP made “brainrot” a badge for skibidi/Ohio/67-style nonsense culture in the mid-2020s.

entries.short: Invisible cool-points — you gain or lose aura based on how a moment lands.
entries.explain: “Aura farming” = doing things that look effortlessly cool. Losing aura = the moment was embarrassing.
entries.origin: Gaming/stream “aura” talk → TikTok scoring social moments like an RPG stat (2024–).

entries.short: Over-praising someone — hype that feels excessive.
entries.explain: Callout for bootlicking energy. Not about donuts.
entries.origin: AAVE/rap slang → TikTok captions and live chat.

entries.short: Doomed, in trouble, or exhausted — the situation is already over.
entries.explain: ‘You’re cooked’ means you messed up or you’re about to. Opposite energy of ‘let him cook’ (let them cook = let them cook / they’re on a roll). Tone is usually playful panic.
entries.origin: Internet slang; sports and school chats use it constantly.

entries.short: Talking a lot — chatter, rant, or playful overshare.
entries.explain: Can be affectionate (“let her yap”) or “please stop yapping.”
entries.origin: Older slang revived as TikTok/stream chat vocabulary.

entries.short: Lose composure — spiral, fight, or emotionally explode.
entries.explain: Can be literal drama or exaggerated “I almost crashed out.”
entries.origin: AAVE → TikTok/Twitter mainstream.

entries.short: Gen Alpha / TikTok brainrot catchphrase — yelled for the bit, not a literal code.
entries.explain: Kids shout ‘six seven’ with a hand gesture because the sound/meme is the joke. There isn’t a hidden dictionary meaning; participating in the noise is the point. You’re not late for asking.
entries.origin: TikTok sounds (notably Skrilla’s “Doot Doot (6 7)”) and hallway copycat energy.

entries.explain: Praise word. Context usually taste or vibe.
entries.origin: AAVE → wider Gen Z/TikTok use.

entries.short: Fully focused — no distractions, main-character concentration.
entries.explain: Sports/grind phrase for deep focus (studying, competing, performing).
entries.origin: Sports and gaming focus talk → TikTok study/grind culture catchphrase.

entries.short: Don’t interrupt — they’re onto something (hype green light).
entries.explain: Give them room to finish the play, rant, or idea. “Who let him cook?” is the confused/chaotic variant.
entries.origin: Lil B “let that boy cook” (c. 2010) → sports Twitter (“Let Russ cook,” Russell Wilson) → general TikTok/internet hype phrase.

entries.short: Laughing out loud (or a softer chuckle online).
entries.explain: Originally meant actual laughing. Now it's often just a softener — 'lol ok' can mean acknowledgment, awkwardness, or mild amusement. LMAO / LMFAO are louder variants. Nobody is judging you for using it; almost everyone does.
entries.origin: Early internet / SMS culture, 1980s–90s Usenet and chat rooms.

entries.explain: A wink that the joke or reference is for people already in on it. Used in captions when explaining would kill the vibe. Related energy: 'you had to be there.'
entries.origin: Social captions and stan Twitter; now everywhere.

entries.short: Charisma / flirting game — “W rizz” good, “L rizz” bad.
entries.explain: Can be serious compliment or joke. Oxford’s 2023 Word of the Year spotlight cemented it.
entries.origin: Popularized by Kai Cenat and stream culture; exploded on TikTok; Oxford Word of the Year 2023.

entries.short: The problem is your skill, not the game (or situation).
entries.explain: Gaming roast that escaped into general life: failed a task? Skill issue. Often joking.
entries.origin: Competitive gaming / Twitch chat dunk → general meme slang in the early 2020s.

entries.short: Acting scripted/basic — like a non-player character.
entries.explain: Can mean unoriginal vibes or the political “NPC meme.” Context matters.
entries.origin: Gaming term → meme culture/TikTok personality shorthand.

entries.short: Good game — polite match ending (EZ = toxic gloat).
entries.explain: GG is sportsmanship after a match. GG EZ (easy) is a taunt. Many communities frown on EZ spam. Alone, GG still means 'respect, match over.'
entries.origin: Competitive gaming etiquette.

entries.short: Log off and go outside / reconnect with reality.
entries.explain: Tells someone they’re too online. Can be mean or affectionate depending on delivery.
entries.origin: Meme/gaming spaces (esp. early 2020s) → mainstream internet advice-as-insult.

entries.short: Delusional (often about a crush) — sometimes worn proudly.
entries.explain: “Delulu is the solulu” = staying hopeful on purpose.
entries.origin: K-pop / stan spaces → TikTok mainstream.

entries.explain: FOMO is anxiety that others are having more fun. JOMO is the flip: pleasure in missing the party on purpose. Both show up in wellness and social media discourse.
entries.origin: Marketing / social media vocabulary (2000s–2010s).

entries.short: Killed it — look, performance, or confidence is elite.
entries.explain: Compliment with ballroom/queer roots. Tone can be sincere or campy.
entries.origin: Ballroom and LGBTQ+ vernacular → viral TikTok/Twitter.

entries.short: Cap = lie; no cap = not lying / for real.
entries.explain: Truth marker or accusation of faking. Extremely common in captions and comments.
entries.origin: AAVE (“cap” = lie) → mainstream Gen Z/TikTok; “no cap” became a default honesty tag in the late 2010s–2020s.
AAVE → mainstream youth slang.

entries.short: Suspicious — popularized hard by Among Us.
entries.explain: Something or someone feels off. Among Us made it ubiquitous; still used for anything shady or questionable.
entries.origin: Older slang; exploded with Among Us (2020).

entries.short: Unapologetically authentic — agreeing with a bold take (tone varies by community).
entries.explain: Praise for saying the quiet part or refusing to soften an opinion. Meaning drifts by subculture; sometimes political, often just “respect.”
entries.origin: Lil B’s positive “based” → 4chan/meme spread and wider internet; still a default agree-stamp.
Gen Z slang / gaming adjacent → mainstream dismissive adjective.

entries.explain: High praise for a look, verse, speech, or read.
entries.origin: Black Twitter / LGBTQ+ slang → TikTok mainstream.

entries.explain: BRB = be right back; AFK = away from keyboard; TTYL = talk to you later; IMO/IMHO = in my (humble) opinion; TBH = to be honest; IDK = I don't know; SMH = shaking my head; NVM = never mind; OMG / WTF = surprise / frustration. Old-school but still everywhere.
entries.origin: Early chat rooms, SMS, and forums.

entries.short: Playful TikTok confession formats: snack-plate meals or joke purchase logic.
entries.explain: Girl dinner = snack plate as a meal; girl/boy math = pseudologic justifying spending. Light meme, not a rulebook.
entries.origin: TikTok trend/confession formats (girl dinner ~2023; girl math alongside).

entries.short: Living like the protagonist of your own story.
entries.explain: Can mean confidence and presence, or gentle teasing that someone’s treating mundane life like a movie.
entries.origin: TikTok “main character” trend/self-help-adjacent meme culture (~2020–).

entries.short: When replies (or quote-tweets) crush likes — a public dunk metric.
entries.explain: On Twitter/X, a bad take “gets ratioed.” People reply “ratio” to try to make it happen.
entries.origin: Twitter culture (2010s–); became a primary clapback mechanic before migrating to other apps as metaphor.
